subject: ss-paediatric-surgery
title: Paediatric oncology and urology: Wilms tumour, neuroblastoma, germ cell tumours and hydronephrosis

steps.tx: **Wilms tumour** is the commonest primary renal malignancy of childhood, striking roughly 1 in 10000 children between ages 2 and 4 years. It presents as a firm painless flank mass that still feels smooth on palpation. Unlike neuroblastoma, it often remains confined by a pseudocapsule. About 5 to 10 percent of cases are bilateral and need careful planning.
steps.say: Look at Wilms tumour as the classic kidney tumour of toddlers and preschool children. Families usually notice a painless lump in the tummy during bathing rather than pain or fever. The mass tends to feel smooth and well defined because it grows inside its own capsule, and this behaviour helps you separate it from neuroblastoma on imaging.

steps.tx: Genetic predisposition accounts for **8 percent of Wilms tumours**, including Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, WAGR syndrome with WT1 deletion, and Denys-Drash syndrome. WT1 mutations on chromosome 11p13 drive tumour formation. Sporadic disease is more common and occurs in about 92 percent of children. Family history raises risk but most children have no family history at all.
steps.say: Consider how genetics shapes risk in a small minority of children with Wilms tumour. Syndromes with overgrowth or deleted gene copies on chromosome eleven carry much higher chances, so any child with a flank mass plus overgrowth features needs careful counselling. Most cases arise on their own without any family story, so absence of a family history never excludes the diagnosis.

steps.tx: COG staging for **Wilms tumour uses 5 stages**: stage 1 confined to kidney, stage 2 breach into perinephric tissue, stage 3 regional nodes or rupture, stage 4 haematogenous spread mainly to lungs, and stage 5 bilateral disease. Postoperative staging after surgery decides chemotherapy intensity. Bilateral stage 5 disease in 5 percent of children is staged per kidney and treated with preservation intent.
steps.say: Understand staging as the roadmap that decides chemotherapy layers for Wilms tumour. Early stages stay local and need limited drugs, while nodal spread or lung spread pushes therapy upward. Spill at surgery matters, so the surgeon avoids rupture and sends nodes for review. Bilateral disease is staged on both sides and managed to save kidney tissue wherever possible.

steps.tx: Clinical features include **abdominal mass in 85 percent**, hypertension in 20 percent from renin secretion, and haematuria in 15 percent of children. The mass does not cross the midline and shows semicircular displacement of bowel. Varicocele or severe pain suggests venous extension. About 4 percent present with pulmonary metastases at diagnosis, so chest imaging is mandatory.
steps.say: Notice the typical story of a child with a silent flank lump and surprisingly good health. Blood pressure is often high, urine may look pink, and the lump stays separate from the midline structures. Cross midline growth or a calcified woody mass points instead toward neuroblastoma, so do not delay cross sectional imaging once you feel such a lump.

steps.tx: Imaging starts with **abdominal ultrasound detecting 95 percent** of masses plus Doppler for venous thrombus. CT chest identifies lung metastases in 4 percent and guides chemotherapy. Tumour markers include LDH and renal vein invasion predicts nodal disease. MIBG scan is not routine for Wilms tumour but remains essential when neuroblastoma is the alternative diagnosis in doubt.
steps.say: Picture the workup as ultrasound first to confirm the kidney origin and venous run, then chest CT to hunt lung deposits. Renal vein spread predicts nodal disease and changes risk grouping, so report it clearly. If the mass crosses the midline or encases vessels, step back and test for neuroblastoma markers and MIBG uptake before committing to a Wilms pathway.

steps.tx: Modern COG therapy uses **preoperative vincristine and dactinomycin for 6 weeks** to shrink tumour and reduce rupture from 30 percent to about 5 percent. Nephroureterectomy with node sampling follows chemotherapy. Radiotherapy of 10.8 Gy in 6 fractions suits stage 3 fields. Doxorubicin is added for unfavourable histology with 1p loss in roughly 12 percent of children.
steps.say: Recall that many centres shrink the tumour with chemotherapy first, which makes the later operation safer and lowers spillage. The ipsilateral node packet is always sampled because staging depends on it. Radiotherapy is reserved for defined fields, and doxorubicin joins only when histology reads unfavourable. This sequence has lifted survival above ninety percent for typical disease.

steps.tx: **Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest** tissue, with 60 percent adrenal primaries and 30 percent extra adrenal. It is the commonest extracranial solid tumour of infancy, with median age 17 months. MYCN amplification in 20 percent signals high risk behaviour. Catecholamines rise in 90 percent of children and support the diagnosis alongside imaging and histology.
steps.say: Turn next to neuroblastoma as a tumour of the immature nervous system, most often starting in the adrenal gland. It grows by wrapping around vessels and crossing the midline, which surgeons view with caution. Excess catecholamines in most children cause flushing and bounding pulses, and MYCN amplification marks the aggressive group that needs intensive therapy.

steps.tx: Risk stratification follows **INSS and INRG criteria with MYCN status** and 1p deletion predicts poor outcome. Low risk tumours under 18 months may regress with observation alone. Intermediate risk shows spotty calcification in 80 percent. High risk disease needs myeloablative therapy with autologous rescue. Stage 4S in 5 percent of infants can regress spontaneously despite skin and liver spread.
steps.say: Stratify neuroblastoma by age, stage, and genetics rather than by size alone. A small infant with localised disease and no MYCN amplification may do well with modest therapy, while an amplified tumour in an older child needs full high risk protocols. Babies with stage four S pattern often improve even without aggressive treatment, which is a classic examination trap.

steps.tx: **Germ cell tumours in children favour sacrococcygeal sites** in 40 percent, with gonadal sites next. Sacrococcygeal teratomas appear in about 1 in 35000 live births and grow faster than 2 cm per month when malignant. Serum AFP rises above 10000 ng per mL in yolk sac elements. HCG rises in choriocarcinoma components and guides chemotherapy choice.
steps.say: Look closely at sacrococcygeal germ cell tumours because they outnumber ovarian germ cell tumours in early childhood. These sacral masses may be largely hidden inside the pelvis, so a careful rectal examination matters. Rising AFP tells you about yolk sac change, while rising HCG suggests a different pattern, and both markers shape the chemotherapy plan.

steps.tx: Antenatal hydronephrosis is seen in **about 1 percent of pregnancies** and needs postnatal ultrasound at 7 days when severe. Pelviureteric junction obstruction is the commonest cause in 30 percent. SFU grade 3 or 4 dilation with poor drainage needs diuretic renogram. Infantile UTI with 5 percent VUR in grade 3 or higher warrants micturating cystogram.
steps.say: Follow antenatal hydronephrosis into the first week with a targeted Doppler ultrasound of the kidneys. Most mild dilation settles, but severe pelvic fullness suggests a junction problem that can damage growing kidney. Febrile urinary infection in an infant deserves a cystogram when the ultrasound already shows high grade reflux, because scarring risks later hypertension.

steps.tx: Complications include **renal impairment in 10 percent after nephrectomy**, late fertility effects from flank radiation, and doxorubicin cardiotoxicity near 5 percent at 5 years. Rhabdoid tumours with SMARCB1 loss behave aggressively despite small size. VACTERL association appears in about 1 in 3 children with anorectal malformations. Second tumours affect 3 percent of long term Wilms survivors.
steps.say: Keep in mind the long term price of cure in childhood abdominal tumours. Kidney function needs lifelong checks after nephrectomy, and the heart needs surveillance after anthracyclines. Late second cancers are uncommon but real, so follow up never fully ends. A rapidly growing rhabdoid tumour deserves urgent theatre time because it spreads weeks earlier than Wilms.

steps.tx: **Wilms tumour survival exceeds 90 percent** with stage directed chemotherapy, while 4S neuroblastoma in infants often regresses under observation. Sacrococcygeal teratomas need coccygectomy to prevent recurrence near 15 percent. Severe antenatal hydronephrosis in 1 percent needs day 7 scanning. Lung metastases in 4 percent of Wilms cases trigger stage 4 therapy.
steps.say: High-yield for the exam, remember the numbers that separate these tumours: Wilms peaks at two to four years with smooth masses, neuroblastoma peaks at under one year and crosses the midline, and sacrococcygeal teratomas favour newborn sacral sites with raised AFP. Grade three reflux and solitary kidney with hydronephrosis always need prompted cystogram and renogram pathways in viva answers.
